shoebill.life: Shoebills are mostly solitary, even outside the breeding season, and each bird keeps to its own patch of swamp. They prefer murky, poorly oxygenated water, where fish such as lungfish must rise to the surface to breathe, making them easier to catch. A shoebill will sometimes move to a new spot by flying low over the reeds, its huge wings flapping slowly; it flaps only about 150 times a minute, one of the slowest wingbeats of any bird. On hot days, shoebills cool themselves by fluttering the skin of their throats.
shoebill.anatomy: Shoebills have unusually long legs and toes for a bird their size, and they can stand on one leg for long periods. Their plumage is a soft slate grey, darker on the back, and young birds are browner. Their eyes, which may be bluish in young birds, turn pale yellow or grey as they age, giving adults their famously unsettling stare. Despite their bulky look, they weigh only around 4 to 7 kilograms.

aye-aye.life: An aye-aye may travel more than a kilometre in a night, moving through the canopy and sometimes along the ground. It builds several nests in its home range, sleeping in a different one on different days. Males have large, overlapping home ranges, while females keep smaller areas apart from each other. Aye-ayes communicate with scent marks and a range of calls, including a sharp 'ey-ey' that may be the origin of their name.
aye-aye.anatomy: The aye-aye's large ears can swivel independently, helping it pinpoint the faint sounds of insect larvae moving inside wood. Its eyes are adapted to see in very low light. Its incisor teeth are coated with hard enamel only on the front, so they wear into sharp chisels. The skin of its hands is sensitive, and its unusual thumb-like extra digit on each wrist, discovered only in 2019, may help it grip branches.

saiga.life: Saigas move in a distinctive way, running with their heads held low, which may help them breathe the dusty steppe air. They need to drink in summer, so herds often travel to lakes and rivers, but they can also get water from plants and snow. Wolves and, for calves, foxes, eagles and stray dogs are their main predators. Harsh winters with deep snow or ice crusts can cause large numbers to starve.
saiga.anatomy: In winter, a saiga's coat becomes long, thick and pale, nearly white, with a fluffy fringe along the belly, keeping out temperatures well below minus 30 degrees. In summer, it moults to a short, thin, sandy coat. The male's horns are slightly translucent and ringed with ridges. During the rut, a male's nose swells even larger and is thought to help amplify his roaring calls to impress females.

star-nosed-mole.life: Star-nosed moles are active day and night, all year round, and they don't hibernate. In winter, they hunt under ice in ponds and streams and travel through tunnels beneath the snow. Their tunnels often lead into water, and they can swim using all four feet and their tail. Their main predators include hawks, owls, foxes, skunks, weasels and large fish such as pike, which can catch them while they swim.
star-nosed-mole.anatomy: The star is not used for digging; when burrowing, the mole folds its rays over its nostrils to protect them. Each of the 22 rays is numbered by scientists, and the two lowest, small rays, numbers 11, work like a fovea, the sharp centre of an eye: the mole moves its star to touch interesting objects with these rays for a closer feel. Its brain devotes an enormous area to processing touch from the star.

hoatzin.life: Hoatzins are noisy and social, living in groups of up to several dozen birds. They hiss, groan and croak, and their wheezing calls fill riverbanks at dawn and dusk. Because their food takes so long to digest, they spend much of the day perched, often resting their full crops on a special patch of hard skin on their breastbone, like a built-in cushion. They rarely fly more than a few dozen metres at a time.
hoatzin.people: Some Indigenous communities in the Amazon have traditionally eaten hoatzin eggs, and in parts of the region the birds' feathers and other body parts were used in folk remedies. Scientists who analysed the hoatzin's digestive system in the 1980s and 1990s were surprised to find bacteria and chemistry so similar to cattle's. The hoatzin's odd appearance has made it a favourite in children's books about strange animals.

pink-fairy-armadillo.life: Pink fairy armadillos are thought to be mostly solitary and nocturnal, emerging to the surface after dark, especially after rain, when the soil is soft. They have been seen moving through sand by sweeping their front claws in a swimming motion, almost like breaststroke. Their low body temperature and slow metabolism may help them save energy in the harsh desert climate, where nights can be cold and days very hot.
pink-fairy-armadillo.people: Because it rarely survives in captivity, very few pink fairy armadillos have ever been kept in zoos, and none have lived there long. Researchers in Argentina have begun using hair samples, footprints and reports from rural communities to map where it lives. Social media has turned it into an online celebrity, prompting scientists to remind people that admiring it from afar is the best way to help.

fossa.life: Fossas have large home ranges, which can exceed 20 square kilometres for males. They are active at different times of day depending on the season and prey availability. On the ground, they move with a bounding gait; in trees, they can leap gaps of several metres. They are skilled at hunting sifakas, among the largest lemurs, sometimes chasing them through the canopy at high speed.
fossa.anatomy: A fossa's head looks somewhat like a puma's, with large, forward-facing eyes and prominent whiskers. Its retractable claws are curved and sharp, and its tail is nearly the length of its body, acting as a counterweight when climbing. Fossas have well-developed scent glands under the tail and on the chest, used to mark their territory. They can rotate their hind feet to grip tree trunks.

dhole.life: Dholes often hunt in the early morning and late afternoon, when it is cooler. Pack members spread out through the forest and use calls to coordinate, sometimes driving deer into water where they can be surrounded. After a kill, they eat quickly, allowing young members to feed first. Dholes are also known to den in communal burrows, and packs can include several adults helping with pups.
dhole.anatomy: Dholes have relatively short legs and a long body, with large rounded ears that help them hear in dense forest. Their coat varies from rusty red in the south to paler, thicker fur in colder regions. They have a broad, short muzzle and strong jaws, and their teeth are adapted for slicing meat rather than crushing bone. Their bushy tail often ends in a black tip.

wolverine.life: Wolverines are mostly solitary, but they are known to keep in touch with family members and sometimes share food. They use scent marking extensively, leaving musky signals on trees, rocks and caches. In winter, they can travel tens of kilometres in a day across snow, and their large feet let them move easily where other predators sink. They are active day and night, alternating periods of activity and rest.
wolverine.anatomy: Wolverines have a strong sense of smell, able to locate carcasses buried under deep snow. Their jaws and neck muscles are powerful enough to crush bone and tear frozen meat. Their claws are semi-retractable, helping them climb trees and steep rock. A wolverine's thick fur is dark brown, with light stripes along the sides that meet above the tail, and many have a pale patch on the chest.

kea.life: Kea are highly social, especially young birds, which roam in groups exploring and testing everything around them. Adults defend territories during the breeding season. Kea can survive harsh alpine winters, feeding on roots, seeds and insects buried in snow or rock. They are known to dig up the roots of mountain plants and to visit carcasses of sheep or deer, which once fuelled their bad reputation with farmers.
kea.anatomy: Kea have strong legs and feet for walking and hopping across rocks and snow, and they rarely need to fly far. Their olive-green feathers are edged with dark lines, giving a scaled look, while their underwings and rump flash bright orange-red in flight. Their long, curved upper beak is sharp and powerful, and their tongue is muscular, helping them manipulate objects with surprising precision.

secretarybird.life: Secretarybirds walk across grasslands in a slow, deliberate way, stamping on tufts of grass to flush out prey. When they spot a snake, they jump and kick repeatedly, aiming for the head. They often hunt in pairs or small family groups. At night they fly up to roost in trees, usually acacias, and they return to the ground in the morning to hunt again.
secretarybird.anatomy: A secretarybird's legs are long, with thick scales protecting the lower legs from snake bites. Its head looks like an eagle's, with a hooked beak and large eyes framed by orange-red skin and long eyelashes. Its tail has two very long central feathers that trail behind in flight. Despite its height, a secretarybird weighs only around 3 to 4 kilograms.

superb-lyrebird.life: Male superb lyrebirds sing most intensely in winter, when they are trying to attract females, and some may sing for hours each day. Their songs mix their own calls with mimicry of other birds, and young males learn their repertoire by listening to older males. Females also sing and mimic, though less often. Lyrebirds are mostly solitary outside the breeding season and defend territories.
superb-lyrebird.people: In the 1930s, lyrebirds in Sherbrooke Forest near Melbourne became famous for letting visitors come close, and they have since starred in many documentaries. Recordings of lyrebirds near towns copying car alarms, construction noise and camera clicks are regularly shared online. Tourists visiting Sherbrooke Forest near Melbourne can sometimes see them close to the walking tracks.

gharial.life: Gharials spend most of their time in water, coming out only to bask and nest. They need deep pools where they can swim and hide, and sandy riverbanks where they can sun themselves. In winter, they bask for longer periods to warm up. They are mostly solitary, though they gather at good basking sites. Their population has been affected by changes in river flow due to dams.
gharial.anatomy: A gharial's long snout is lined with about 110 sharp, interlocking teeth, ideal for gripping slippery fish. Its eyes and nostrils sit on top of its head, so it can watch and breathe while mostly submerged. Its body is olive green to grey, and its back is armoured with bony plates. The male's ghara grows as he matures and is a sign of breeding maturity.

thorny-devil.life: Thorny devils are slow-moving and active mostly in mild weather, avoiding the hottest and coldest parts of the day. They shelter in shallow burrows they dig themselves or under bushes. They often return to the same ant trails to feed, eating ant after ant for long periods. Their main predators include birds such as bustards, and goannas.
thorny-devil.anatomy: The thorny devil's spikes are made of keratin and grow from its scales. Its colour can change slightly, becoming paler in warm weather and darker when it is cold or stressed, helping it control body temperature and blend in. The grooves between its scales act like tiny straws, drawing water by capillary action. Its tail is also covered in spikes.

blandings-turtle.life: Blanding's turtles are often seen basking on logs, sedge tussocks and muskrat lodges in spring. They move between different wetlands during the year, using some for feeding, others for overwintering and nesting. They are most active in the morning and late afternoon. Their slow movement on land makes them vulnerable when crossing roads, especially during the nesting season in June.
blandings-turtle.anatomy: Blanding's turtle has a high, rounded shell and a long neck that it can stretch far out of its shell. The hinge on its plastron lets it partially close its shell, although adults cannot shut it completely like box turtles. Its yellow throat and chin are bright and easy to spot. Hatchlings are dark grey, with a less domed shell, and gain their yellow spots as they grow.
